edge_cases.scenario: A collector places 10 calls in five days about one debt; three ring with no answer because the consumer's number was out of service, and two are answered by an automated carrier message rather than the subscriber. The consumer sues, pointing to the call log showing 10 attempts.
edge_cases.gap_description: The logic excludes 'calls not connected to the dialed number,' but the completeness checklist asks only for 'dates/times of all calls' and never asks whether each call actually connected, went to voicemail, or was a limited-content message. Without per-call connection status, the dispositive facts collected are insufficient to compute the count the rule requires, and no fact element distinguishes a connected voicemail (counts) from an unconnected attempt (does not).

edge_cases.scenario: A collector's letter tells the consumer, "Your refusal to pay this bill constitutes theft of services and check fraud," and adds that once the account is sold to a purchaser next month the consumer "will lose any right to dispute or assert defenses." The consumer sues under §1692e.
edge_cases.gap_description: The catalog omits §1692e(6) (falsely representing that a sale/transfer of the debt will cause the consumer to lose a claim or defense, or become subject to prohibited practices) and §1692e(7) (falsely representing that the consumer committed a crime or other conduct to disgrace the consumer). The list jumps from (5) to (8), so a pattern squarely within the statute has no matching item; only the residual (10) catch-all could be strained to reach it, and the completeness checklist never asks about accusations of criminality or representations about the effect of transferring the debt.

edge_cases.scenario: A collection law firm files a state-court complaint against the consumer to collect the debt. The complaint and the summons contain no statement that the sender is a debt collector, and no prior letter had been sent; the consumer claims a §1692e(11) mini-Miranda violation.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist treats the mini-Miranda disclosure as dispositive in the initial and every subsequent communication, but §1692e(11) expressly exempts "a formal pleading made in connection with a legal action," and Reg F §1006.18(e)(3) carries forward that exclusion. No checklist item captures the communication's form or litigation context (pleading vs. dunning letter), so the encoded rule would generate a false positive. Relatedly, the checklist never asks who received the communication (consumer vs. court, employer, or credit bureau), which also matters for which subsections apply.

edge_cases.scenario: A dunning letter correctly states the balance and creditor but misidentifies the original creditor's corporate suffix ("ABC Bank, N.A." instead of "ABC Bank, FSB") and overstates accrued interest by $0.03. The consumer concedes she understood exactly who was collecting and what she owed, but sues under §1692e(2)(A) and (10).
edge_cases.gap_description: The catalog's "any single item, if the facts match, is an independent violation" framing has no materiality filter and no articulation of the objective standard (least sophisticated / unsophisticated consumer) that most circuits apply to §1692e. The checklist asks only for exact wording, not whether the falsehood was material or capable of influencing a consumer's decision, so literal but trivial inaccuracies would be scored as violations. The checklist also omits the §1692k(c) bona fide error defense and threshold coverage facts (whether the actor is a 'debt collector' and the obligation a 'consumer debt').

edge_cases.scenario: A part-time debtor in a city with a $19.36 local minimum wage has $700 in weekly disposable earnings. 48 x $19.36 = $929.28, so prong two is 40% of (-$229.28) = -$91.71, while prong one is $140. Taking 'the lesser of the two prongs' literally yields a negative maximum garnishment, and the employer's payroll system withholds nothing but the creditor argues the negative result should be read as an offset or that prong one controls.
edge_cases.gap_description: The formula has no floor at zero and no stated rule for when disposable earnings fall at or below 48x the applicable minimum wage. edge_cases.gap_description: The rule treats the carve-out as a binary classification of the judgment ('ordinary debt judgment vs. wages/support judgment'), but judgments are frequently mixed. edge_cases.scenario: The creditor could not locate the debtor for in-person delivery, so the justice court authorized service by posting the citation on the door under Rule 501.2(e) (or substituted service under Rule 106). The petition was posted on March 3 and the debtor found it March 10.
edge_cases.gap_description: Both the logic ('deadline_computed_from: date of service (delivery by constable or process server)') and the checklist assume personal delivery. They provide no trigger date for alternative service methods (posting, mailing, publication, Rule 106(b) substituted service), where the operative date is the date of posting/mailing/publication rather than actual receipt, and where some methods carry a different answer window entirely. The rule as encoded either fails to fire or silently uses the wrong start date.

edge_cases.scenario: A debt buyer sues in justice court for $19,400 in principal but the petition also demands $1,800 in contractual pre-judgment interest and $2,500 in attorney's fees, for a total prayer of $23,700. The user answers the checklist question 'amount claimed in the suit' with $23,700.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist asks for 'amount claimed' without specifying that the $20,000 justice-court ceiling is measured exclusive of interest and costs (and with contested treatment of attorney's fees). A user reporting the gross prayer will be told justice court doesn't apply even though it does. The node also has no branch for what happens when the ceiling genuinely is exceeded — the county/district court answer deadline is materially different (Monday after 20 days from service), so the rule fails open with no fallback.

edge_cases.scenario: The 14th day after service falls on a Friday when the county courthouse is closed under a local four-day-workweek order (or closed for an ice storm), which is not a state legal holiday. The defendant files the following Monday.
edge_cases.gap_description: The logic's extension trigger is 'weekend or court holiday,' which is broader and vaguer than TRCP 4's actual trigger ('Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday'). Texas has no express clerk's-office-inaccessibility extension analogous to FRCP 6(a)(3), so the encoded rule may wrongly tell a defendant a locally-closed day is auto-extended. Conversely the checklist collects no fact about court closures or local holiday calendars, so the extension branch cannot be evaluated at all from the listed inputs.
